analysis.one_liner: Lets people control who collects and sells their COVID-19 health data and bans its use in ads and discrimination.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 12 senators backing it but never received a hearing, markup, or vote in the Senate Health Committee, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: During the pandemic, apps and websites for contact tracing and symptom checking were collecting sensitive health data — test results, location, who you were near — largely outside the main federal health privacy law, HIPAA. This bill would have required companies to get clear consent before collecting that data, barred them from using it for advertising or to discriminate in jobs, housing, credit, or insurance, forced large data holders to publish reports about how they use it, and required the data to be destroyed after the emergency. It let the Federal Trade Commission, state attorneys general, and individuals enforce the rules in court, including through class actions.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who used COVID-19 apps, screening tools, or any service that gathered health data. The bill would have stopped their test results, location history, and contact networks from being sold for advertising or used to deny them jobs, housing, credit, insurance, or even the right to vote.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People using COVID-19 apps and services

how_it_helps.text: Required organizations to get clear, affirmative consent before collecting, using, or selling emergency health data such as test results, location, proximity, and contact information [S3].
Prohibited using that data for commercial advertising, e-commerce, or to make employment, housing, credit, insurance, or education opportunities unavailable based on health status [S3].
Barred government and companies from denying or interfering with the right to vote based on health data, and let individuals sue to enforce it [S3].

Gave the FTC, state attorneys general, and individuals the power to sue violators, and made pre-dispute arbitration clauses unenforceable for these claims, preserving access to court and class actions [S3].
Required organizations holding data on 100,000 or more people to publicly report every 90 days how they collect, use, and share it, and required destruction of the data after the emergency ends [S3].

analysis.who_pays: App developers, contact-tracing technology companies, data brokers, and advertisers would bear compliance costs and lose access to a large pool of pandemic-era health and location data they were monetizing.
analysis.who_pays_short: App makers, data brokers, and advertisers

drawbacks.text: Consent requirements, security mandates, and strict data destruction timelines would have imposed real compliance costs on app developers and could have slowed rollout or updating of contact-tracing and screening tools during an emergency [S3].

The private right of action with statutory damages of $100 to $5,000 per violation and no preemption of state law would have invited waves of class-action litigation, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge [S3].

The bill excluded HIPAA-covered health providers and public health authorities, leaving the main health system under older privacy rules and creating two parallel regimes that could confuse patients about their rights [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — keeping sensitive pandemic health data out of ad networks and away from landlords, employers, and insurers — was significant and the bill was carefully scoped: it exempted public health authorities, health providers, and legitimate research, so the pandemic response could continue. The genuine costs were the compliance and litigation burden on app developers, and the risk that strict rules made some useful health tools slower to build.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Blumenthal introduced the bill on January 28, 2021 with 11 cosponsors — 10 Democrats and 1 independent — all from the same two caucuses [S1].
It was read twice and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day, which was its last recorded action [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action appears anywhere in its two-year action history [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers, advertisers, and app operators who kept collecting and monetizing pandemic-era health and location data without the consent rules, disclosure requirements, or litigation exposure this bill would have imposed. Individuals whose health data was collected also remain without the private right of action or arbitration protection this bill offered.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its push in the Senate

for.name: 10 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate independents
for.role: Original cosponsors (incl. Sens. Warner, Klobuchar, Warren, Durbin, Booker)

against.name: Chair Patty Murray and the Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in committee for its entire two-year history with no action after referral

sides.party_line_note: All 12 original sponsors were Democrats or the independent who caucuses with them; no Senate Republican cosponsored the bill [S4].

industries.note: These companies were collecting and monetizing location, proximity, and health data generated by pandemic apps. The bill would have required consent, barred advertising use, forced public reporting, and opened them to lawsuits — their gain from the bill dying is directly the public's loss of privacy.

They would have gained credibility from consent and security rules but borne compliance costs, mandatory data destruction, and lawsuit exposure under a private right of action. Their interest in operating without these rules ran against users' interest in controlling their data.
The bill barred using emergency health data to make jobs, housing, credit, or insurance unavailable based on health status, closing a screening channel at ordinary people's expense.
The bill made pre-dispute arbitration clauses unenforceable for claims under it, keeping disputes in court where class actions are possible.
